name: Carla Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, thank you for agreeing to this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Is that okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'm not much of a talker, but I'll try.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's fine. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader at an open-cut coal mine, which means a big machine with a bucket on the front that loads coal and dirt into trucks. I'm on day shift this month, so I'm up at four, on the bus at five, and in the seat by six. I'm still the slowest loader on my crew, and the shift boss, Gary, times us, so I feel it. I like that it's simple: fill the truck, next truck, and nobody needs me to be clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That suits me. I don't use any of that AI stuff, so I'd be glad it went nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the bus stop, that all the fuss was for nothing. I don't post online much, so I'd just shrug and say back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means AI isn't my problem, but the mine still is. Nobody at the coal mine is scared of a chatbot. We're scared of the closure date the company keeps not telling us. There's talk it closes in eight or nine years, and I rent alone, so my pay is all there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and try to get faster on the loader so Gary stops timing me. I'd keep putting a bit aside each fortnight, I've got about two months now and I'd like four. I'd probably skip the trip with my cousins at Easter to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, the same as always. Not because of AI, because coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you hear about the closure date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rumours, mostly. Someone's brother works in the office, and he heard 2034, and then someone else heard 2032. The company says nothing's decided, which nobody believes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the closure came, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a couple of other mines within two hours, and the quarry near my mum's place. I'd try those first, I wouldn't want to leave the area.

She'd say it at the **bus stop**, not online, and shrug it off.
think: AI isn't her problem, but the **coal mine closure** still is.
She rents alone, so **her pay** is all there is.
do: Get **faster** on the loader so the shift boss stops timing her.
Grow savings from **two months** to four.
Skip the **Easter trip** with her cousins to save.
feel: **Uneasy** as usual, about coal rather than AI.
S0.quote: Nobody at the coal mine is scared of a chatbot. We're scared of the closure date the company keeps not telling us.
fieldNote: Her steady background worry is the **closure rumour**, not technology.
She lives alone, so a **single income** carries all the risk.
She wants to **stay local**, near her mother, if the mine closes.

steps.text: Get faster on the front-end loader so Gary stops timing her
Grow savings from two months of costs to four
Skip the Easter trip with her cousins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. Slowly to who, though? The trucks here already have collision sensors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not for me, I'll leave it to the young ones who like gadgets. I'd say it at work and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd worry the company picks the machine over me. I've never typed a single question into an AI, and I'm not keen to start because a robot wants my loader. A loader is one of those jobs that looks easy to automate, and I'm the slowest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait to see what the company actually does before I spend money on courses. I'd cut back, no new phone, no takeaway, and get savings to four months. If they offered training I'd go, but I wouldn't chase it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in my stomach. I don't sleep well before a shift as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to training if offered. Would you, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd hate it, and I'd sit at the back, but I'd go. I'm stubborn, not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She worked in the canteen at the old power station until it shut, so she knows what it's like. She'd tell me to stop worrying and save.

fieldNote: She sees herself as the **most replaceable**: slowest operator in a job that looks automatable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before they even close the mine. That's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say someone in charge needs to sort this out, government or the company. I'm not political, but that's too fast for normal people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the robots get my loader around 2031, and I don't know what I'd do. I'd fall back on family. My mum still has my old bedroom, and I can see myself sleeping in it again by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food, and get every dollar I can into savings before 2031. I'd ask about jobs at the quarry and the other mines, even though they'd be going the same way. And I'd talk to my mum about moving back in if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I don't have a plan, and I'm not someone who makes plans fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for if not mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Something with my hands, maybe the council roads crew, or aged care. I've never thought about it because I thought mining was steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the mine you'd turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, maybe, even though he times me. He's been through two layoffs, and he always knows which other site is hiring.

feel: **Sick** and without a plan, and slow to make one.
S2.quote: My mum still has my old bedroom, and I can see myself sleeping in it again by thirty.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and has no alternative career in mind.
The **family home** is her real safety net.
She'd lean on her **shift boss** for leads despite resenting his timing.

steps.text: Cut every cost except rent and food
Ask about jobs at the quarry and the nearby mines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's about when the closure rumour lands anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that someone needs to plan for towns like ours. Maybe I'd sign a petition if someone handed it to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think I'm the first to go. Five years sounds like a lot until you remember I'm still the slowest loader operator on my crew. Having time doesn't help much if I don't use it, and I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get my haul truck ticket too, so I'm not just a loader. I'd keep saving and aim for six months by 2030. And I'd ask my mum's friend who manages the council roads crew if they'd take me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. I lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is about a third of my pay. If I lose the mine wage and get a roads job, it's maybe two-thirds of the money, so the rent eats nearly half. That's where the panic starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move somewhere cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. My mum's here and she's getting older, so I'd rather move in with her than move away.

fieldNote: Five years doesn't calm her, because she **doubts herself** to use the time.

Caring for her **ageing mother** ties her to the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that it isn't next week's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and there's time to work it out. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I could manage. Ten years is enough time to learn a new job, even for someone like me who hates learning new things. And the coal mine probably closes first anyway, so I'd have to move on regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at a trade around 2028 or 2029, probably plant mechanic, fixing machines instead of driving them. I'd save steadily, maybe buy a cheap unit near mum's place with a deposit. And I'd keep driving until the mine shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because I'd have to change, and I hate change. But not up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a mechanic, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad fixed cars in our garage when I was little, and I used to hand him the spanners. Fixing things makes sense to me more than screens do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots not fix machines too, by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But by then I'd be thirty-nine with a unit paid down, and I'd deal with it then. I can't worry about everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, with robots three years later, is just not enough for someone like me. I picked the coal mine because it was steady, and now steady is the one thing nobody can promise. What would help is a straight answer on dates and someone paying for a trade while I'm still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women in mining. It took me years to get this job, and if the jobs go, the women will be the first ones nobody rehires.

headlineQuote: I picked the coal mine because it was steady, and now steady is the one thing nobody can promise.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old loader operator** at an open-cut coal mine, living alone and renting.
She has about **two months saved**, never uses AI and dislikes change.
Her steady worry is the **closure rumour**, so she is uneasy even when AI fizzles.
In fast pictures she has **no plan** and would move back in with her mother.
Given ten years, she imagines becoming a **plant mechanic**, like her father.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too little for someone slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Straight answers** on closure dates and paid **trade training** while still employed.
